newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Labor Dept says CPI modestly overstates inflation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Labor Dept says CPI modestly overstates inflation.

text.p: The Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics Friday conceded that its key Consumer Price Index overstates inflation, but by less than the 1.1 percentage point estimated by an independent panel.

In a formal response to the Boskin Commission study released last December, BLS researchers specifically dismissed about half of the 1.1 point estimate, and said that much of the other half could not be estimated.
"I have to caution you, there is a great deal of uncertainty about the other pieces," Kenneth Dalton, BLS Associate Commissioner for prices and living conditions, told reporters.
Dalton and other BLS officials presented their response to the analysis of a panel led by Stanford University economist Michael Boskin at a hearing of the Joint Economic Commission of Congress.
The BLS charged the Boskin commission with making numerous inaccurate inferences based on faulty or incomplete data.
"The BLS specifically rejects several of the estimated ... biases, in cases where the commission presented new evidence," the study's authors said.
Dalton agreed that substitution bias -- the failure to account for consumers switching among products when prices shift -- artifically boosts CPI by about 0.4 percent a year.
But the BLS report questioned several other Boskin conclusions, saying that the answers in many cases simply cannot be determined.
"There's such a degree of uncertainty ... we as a statistical agency cannot say," said Dalton.
For example, BLS cited huge uncertainties in gauging inflation in the mercurial health care sector, which could cause extensive understatement or overstatement.
"It's not inconceivable that medical care could blow everything out of the water," Dalton said.
The BLS findings appear to affirm Congress' decision not to mandate reduced inflation calculations in a resolution to balance the federal budget passed earlier this spring.
CPI is used to determine annual increases in federal benefits like Social Security and to adjust individual tax payments to account for inflation.
Several prominent politicians and economists, including Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, have suggested the federal deficit could be slashed by billions of dollars by lowering the CPI.

"It would seem rather than making an ad hoc legislative adjustment, leaving it to the BLS to make the adjustment has made sense to us since the Boskin commission report came out," said Chris Frenze, executive director at the Joint Economic Committee.

BLS has stepped up its ongoing efforts to upgrade the CPI and is currently publishing an experimental index that showed inflation at 2.9 percent in 1996, less than the official estimate of 3.3 percent.
But the BLS paper asserted that some other CPI upgrade projects would take years to bear fruit, and may never catch up with the fast-paced U.S. economy.
"The solutions to many CPI measurement issues ... must await methodological breakthroughs in economics or improved availability of data," the report concluded.
